comments.body:
This call doesn’t pass an enqueue option, so it uses whatever the user has set as their default for albums or playlists. If that is “play next” or “add”, the album doesn’t replace the queue. It gets added after the current item, so `items[start]` in `_start_play_context` points at the wrong track. When the track URI check fails, the fallback can pick an older copy of the same track elsewhere in the queue. With “add”, nothing starts playing, so `wait_for_media` waits the full 10 seconds before the jump happens. It also starts the first track and then jumps, so every selection opens a stream it throws away straight after.

The queue controller can already do this in one step. Something like `play_media(player_id, uri, option=QueueOption.REPLACE, start_item=track_uri)` starts at the right track and lets you drop the `expect_new_media`, `wait_for_media` and `play_index` steps. If the TV can only send a position and not a track URI, please at least pass `QueueOption.REPLACE` so the queue position and the album position always match.

threads.body: Container playback now explicitly passes QueueOption.REPLACE, and no longer arms or waits for player media after the queue has loaded. I retained indexed selection because a track URI alone cannot distinguish repeated occurrences in a playlist. Four HTTP regressions use the actual MA enqueue/load path with Add and Play next defaults and verify that the old queue is replaced and the selected duplicate occurrence plays. This still uses play_index after replacement for a non-first selection; it does not implement the single-stream start_item optimization.

comments.body: This setter forces the counter back to 1 or 0. That undoes the reason the counter exists, which is so two overlapping commands can’t clear each other’s suppression. Only the tests use it (test_player.py lines 432, 452 and 701 to 723). Could you remove the setter and have those tests use with `player.suppress_ws_notify()` instead?

threads.body: The setter is removed, and the playback, pause and resume tests now use suppress_ws_notify(). The nesting test remains; an additional regression verifies that direct assignment cannot clear an active suppression context.
